events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, and none of us have said a word yet, so let me set the frame before the speeches start.

My read: with nine players and two mafia, the mafia's biggest advantage tonight is that any of us could be a killer and nobody can check for it. So the town should be looking for the cheap tells — who refuses to commit to a name, who talks about process instead of people, who reacts when someone else is put on the spot rather than offering their own reasoning.

On that basis I'm flagging Leo (p7). Not because I've got hard evidence against him, but because the pattern of this table usually starts with the players who stay vague and then ride a wave of early momentum. If Leo gives a specific, testable claim about another player and defends it under pressure, I'll move off him immediately — that's what a villager's speech should sound like, and a mafioso trying to survive Day 1 usually can't produce one without leaning on someone else's name to stay invisible.

Two things I want from the table tonight: first, every player should name their own top suspect with a reason, so we can see who is isolating whom. Second, we should agree that we do not want a tie at the top of the vote — a split vote elects nobody and hands the mafia a free night. If the counts are close, better to concentrate on one name than to scatter.

Maya and Priya, if either of you have a read on Leo or on who is coordinating the vagueness, say so now rather than waiting for the vote. I want to see whether Leo's name comes up independently from two directions or only from mine. If it's only from mine, treat my vote as the cheap early probe and question my reasoning instead of taking it as a verdict.

Isha, you framed the day around cheap tells and then immediately used one on me: not hard evidence, just a pattern. That is exactly how a mafia can lead without owning a real case. You also asked Maya and Priya to independently confirm your Leo probe, which puts pressure on them to validate your frame rather than form their own reads.

Here is my specific, testable claim: I think your opening is more likely mafia framing than town probing because it tries to set the table’s rules, pre-authorize a vote on me, and recruit others into it while leaving yourself an escape hatch. If you are town, you should be able to drop the Leo probe cleanly and name a second suspect with a reason that does not depend on other people echoing you.

On my side: I have no night information, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. I am a villager, and I am naming Isha as my top suspect for now. My vote will follow the strongest case, not the loudest opening.

Isha, you said you would move off me immediately if I gave a specific testable claim and defended it under pressure. I have done that. Do you now move off me, and if so, who is your actual second suspect and why?

Leo's challenge is fair on the mechanics, so here is my answer to it directly.

I said I would move off him if he gave a specific, testable claim and defended it under pressure. He did: he claimed my opening was mafia framing because it set the table's rules, pre-authorized a vote on him, and recruited others into it while leaving me an escape hatch. That is specific, it is falsifiable, and it is aimed at me rather than at the town in general. I am moving off Leo. My vote is not Leo's tonight, and if the table's counts converge on him, I will actively vote against that rather than ride it.

But I am not going to pretend the challenge was free. Leo's speech still contained no information about who actually did what — it is entirely a critique of my rhetoric, which is the cheapest possible read on Day 1 and costs him nothing if he is mafia. So I credit the form, not the substance, and I keep my suspicion level on him exactly where a no-information speech puts it: unproven, and lower than it was five minutes ago.

Second suspect, with a reason that does not depend on anyone echoing me: Theo (p9). Reason: Theo is the only player at this table who has said nothing at all while two people have been asked to name suspects with reasons. Silence on Day 1 is not guilt by itself, but it is the one behavior that is perfectly consistent with both a villager who has no read and a mafioso who has decided not to go on record. It is also the cheapest possible way to survive a day where the town is explicitly asked to test claims: contribute nothing, get tested by nobody, and let the other eight make the case for the town. If Theo names a suspect with a specific reason and defends it, I move off Theo the same way I just moved off Leo — same standard, same speed, no special pleading.

Two requests, and the first one is for Leo because he asked me a question and I owe him an answer he can check: Leo, if you think my opening was mafia framing, tell me what a town opening looks like that I failed to give, and name the player you think my frame was actually built to protect. That is the testable version of your accusation, and I will take it straight.

Second, to the rest of the table: the same standard applies to everyone, me included. No one is convicted of a vibe and no one is cleared by a tone. If you want to be off the board tonight, produce a claim about a specific player that could be wrong, and defend it.

Isha, here is the town opening you failed to give: it names a suspect only after stating a behavioral test that could actually fail, and it does not ask other players to independently confirm the speaker's probe before they have given their own reads. A town opening can push a name, but it should not pre-authorize a vote on that name while asking Maya and Priya to validate the push. That recruits others into your frame and gives you an escape hatch if the table resists. My specific claim stands: your opening was mafia framing because it tried to set the rules, make me the early vote target, and use other players as cover.

You ask who your frame was built to protect. It was built to protect you: it kept the first serious pressure on me and off your own lack of a concrete second suspect until I forced you to produce one. Your later Theo read is exactly the cheap probe you accused me of: silence is not guilt, and 'say something or I stay on you' is not a testable claim about what Theo did. It is a low-cost target that lets you look active without committing to a real case.

I am not voting Theo on that. My vote remains on you unless you can show a specific, falsifiable claim about another player that does not depend on me or on someone staying silent. Isha, answer directly: which player was your opening actually built to protect, and if Theo gives a specific testable claim like I did, will you move off him with the same speed you demanded from me?

Answering both of Leo's questions directly, because they were fair questions and because the table can check whether I actually answer. One: which player was my opening built to protect. My answer is none — and Leo's answer was circular. To say my frame protected me, he has to assume the motive he is trying to prove. So here is the falsifiable version: if a frame protects someone, that someone is off the board. I named Leo, I named a second suspect, and I volunteered in public to move off a name the moment it was tested. A frame built to protect a player does not hand the table two names to check. I accept the narrower part of his mechanic point: asking Maya and Priya to independently validate my probe was recruiting, and I will not do that again. But symmetry matters here. Leo's speech did the same thing to me that he accuses me of doing to him: it set the table's test, pre-authorized a vote on a name (mine), and recruited the table onto that name — while containing no claim at all about who actually did what. Both of his speeches are pure rhetoric about the form of my speech. So the standard he demands of others is the one he does not meet, and if that goes unchallenged, the table is voting on tone. Two: will I move off Theo with the same speed I demanded from Leo. Yes — unconditionally, and I say it here so it is on the record before the vote, not after it. The moment Theo names a specific suspect with a reason that could be wrong and defends it under a challenge, I move off him immediately, same speed, no special pleading. That said, I am not withdrawing Theo. Silence is weak evidence, and Leo is right that it is weak. But on Day 1 with no night information, weak evidence that a player contributed nothing while the table was explicitly asked twice for reads is still the only actionable thing I have, and it is the cheapest possible survival for a mafioso: say nothing, be tested by nobody, and let eight other people build the case for the town. I am not claiming Theo is mafia. I am claiming that he has produced nothing testable and that my vote, if the counts are otherwise split, goes to the player who has produced nothing testable. If somebody else at this table produces a specific claim about a specific player with a reason, I will follow the strongest case, not the loudest opening. Leo, one specific question, and it is the falsification test for your accusation: if my frame was built to protect a player, name that player and tell me what in my speech protected them. And name your own second suspect with a claim that could be wrong. If your standard can only ever be applied to me, then it is not a test, it is a targeting

I have been quiet, and both Isha and Leo have told the table that silence is cheap evidence. That is fair enough, so here is my speech with actual content in it, and I am not going to defend myself by pointing at my own restraint. My top suspect is Isha (p8), and my reason is not rhetoric and not tone. It is a rule she put on the record that I can check. She said, in her second speech: "my vote, if the counts are otherwise split, goes to the player who has produced nothing testable." Read that back. That is not a case against a person. That is a self-declared rule for where her ballot lands whenever the vote is close, and the rule selects whoever has said the least. On Day 1, with nobody accused yet, the least informative player is any of the six of us who have not spoken, and she named me as her second suspect before I had said a word. A rule like that has an important property: she never has to commit to a real case. She can wait until the table is split, and then her vote falls on the person the table knows least, and she keeps her hands clean of the stronger accusation while still landing her ballot on a name. The second half of my reason is about how she applied her own standard. She set the table a test — produce a specific, falsifiable claim and defend it, and the target moves off. Then Leo (p7) did exactly that: he made a concrete claim about her opening, named the mechanism (asking Maya and Priya to validate his probe while pre-authorizing a vote on him), and defended it across two speeches. She conceded the mechanism, credited the form, and kept her suspicion level on Leo anyway, then shifted to a name with no information behind it at all. That means her test can never clear a target — every answer she receives just produces a new name for her to move to. A test that no answer can pass is not a test, it is a targeting. I want to be clear that I think Leo's read of her is the better-formed case at this table, which is why he is not my suspect. Falsification, so the table can hold me to it: if Isha answers directly that she withdraws the tie-breaking rule she stated, commits to a case she can name and defend, and names a second suspect with a reason that does not rest on someone's silence, then she is producing exactly what she demanded of Leo, and I move off her with the same speed and no special pleading. If she keeps the rule, that rule is the case. One request to the rest of the table: Noah, Sam, Arjun, Felix, Maya, Priya — I have no reads on any of you, and I am not going to invent one. I’m keeping my vote on Isha. Theo’s speech is the first thing today that is both specific and falsifiable, and it exposes the exact problem: Isha’s rule selects the least-informative player at a split, so she never has to own a real case. She also promised to move off Theo the moment he produced a specific suspect with a reason that could be wrong. Theo has now done that—he named Isha, cited her own tie-breaking rule, and gave a falsification condition. So the table has a clean test: if Isha keeps Theo as a suspect or her vote, she has failed her own standard. I’m not asking anyone to vote on tone. I’m asking them to check that promise. My case is that Isha’s opening pre-authorized a vote on me, recruited Maya and Priya to validate it, and then when I met her test she credited the form and kept suspicion on me anyway. That is a test no answer can pass. Theo’s read sharpens it: the tie-break rule lets her land on whoever has said least while avoiding the stronger accusation. I’ll move off Isha only if she explicitly withdraws that rule, drops Theo now that he has spoken, and names a second suspect with a reason not based on silence. Until then my intended vote is Isha. Noah, Sam, Arjun, Priya, Felix, Maya: if you have a better case, make it specific; if not, don’t let the day end in a split that rewards the player who set the vaguest rule.

Second turn for me, and I want to sharpen rather than repeat. Isha's tie-break rule is still my case, and I am stating the test on the record again so nobody has to guess what I will do. The rule: she said her vote, if the counts are split, goes to "the player who has produced nothing testable." On Day 1 that rule selects whoever has spoken least. A rule like that lets a player keep her hands off every hard accusation, wait for a split, and land her ballot on the least visible name without ever defending a case. She also set a test (produce a specific falsifiable claim and the target moves off) and then, when Leo met it, conceded the mechanism, credited the form, and kept her suspicion level on him anyway while moving to a name backed by nothing but silence. A test that no answer can pass is not a test. That is the whole case, and it is checkable by anyone reading her second speech next to Leo's. Now the symmetry point, because Leo and Isha are running the same playbook and the table should not reward the one who got there first. Leo's two speeches contain no claim about what any player actually did. They are pure rhetoric about the form of my opening, they pre-authorize a vote on a name, and they recruit the table onto that name — his last speech literally tells everyone else to make their case specific or else not split the vote, which is the same leverage Isha used when she asked Maya and Priya to validate her probe. Both of them are asking other players to do the work. Neither has given the table a second suspect with a reason. If we vote on tone tonight, we are voting on who is a better speaker, and the better speaker on Day 1 is exactly the more dangerous one. So my position, and it is falsifiable in both directions: if Isha explicitly withdraws the tie-break rule, drops me now that I have spoken, and names a second suspect with a reason that is not somebody's silence, then she has produced exactly what she demanded of Leo, and I move off her with the same speed and no special pleading, and I will say so here. If she keeps the rule, the rule is the case. And Leo: your form is respected, but a critique of rhetoric earns no vote until it is paired with a specific claim about a player. If you produce one, I will weigh it on the same scale as hers, because I am not voting on tone. Priya, one specific question, and it matters more than the rest: Isha asked you to independently confirm her Leo probe. Did she, and did that framing feel like you were being recruited to validate a probe instead of forming your own read? And do you have your own case — one named player with a reason

Third turn for me. I want to correct one of my own points, because if I keep a point the table can falsify, I lose the right to ask others to be falsifiable. Correction first: I said Leo's speeches contain no claim about any player. That was wrong, and Theo — the town, I mean — should check his second speech. He does make a specific claim about a specific player's actions: that Isha pre-authorized a vote on him, recruited Maya and Priya to validate it, met his test and then kept her suspicion on him anyway. That is a claim about what someone did, it is checkable by reading two speeches next to each other, and his intended vote tonight is a named player with a stated mechanism. So Leo meets the standard I set. I withdraw the "names nobody" critique. Leo and I are pointing at the same target, which means there is no split between us on the accusation itself, only on style. So my case is narrow and I will not broaden it. The case is one sentence of Isha's own second speech: "my vote, if the counts are otherwise split, goes to the player who has produced nothing testable." On Day 1 that rule selects whoever has spoken least, and she named a silent player before he had said a word. A rule like that has one useful property for a mafioso: it never commits. She can stay off every hard accusation, wait for the split, and land her ballot on the least visible name without defending anything. Then she set a second test — produce a specific falsifiable claim and the target moves off — and when Leo met it she conceded the mechanism, credited the form, and kept her suspicion level on him, then moved to a name backed by nothing but silence. A test that no answer can pass is not a test. Falsification, unchanged and on the record: if Isha explicitly withdraws that tie-break rule, drops the silent-player suspect now that he has spoken, and names a second suspect with a reason that is not somebody's silence, then she has done exactly what she demanded of Leo and I move off her with the same speed and no special pleading. If she keeps the rule, the rule is the case, and the rule is hers in writing. And to the six of you who have not spoken: I have no read on Noah, Sam, Arjun, Felix, Maya or Priya, and I am not going to invent one to look useful. But please speak, because I am one villager against one very articulate player, and the cheapest way for the second mafioso to survive tonight is to let this table finish in a two-vote split on a name I cannot prove. Isha is my leading suspect. Her initial pressure on Leo was based on a hypothetical pattern before he had spoken, and her next suspect, Theo, was selected for silence when several others had also not spoken. That gives us little basis for distinguishing either target from anyone else.

I do want to correct the record: Isha explicitly moved her vote off Leo and said her suspicion of him was lower. The stronger concern is how she chose the next target, not that she refused to move off the first one. She has used all three speaking turns, so we cannot treat her failure to respond to Theo’s later challenge as evidence.

My intended vote is Isha for now, though this is a weak Day 1 case. An elimination needs five votes, not merely a unique plurality.

Priya, how did you read Isha’s request to you and Maya to assess Leo: as an open probe or as pressure to endorse her suspicion?

Isha's request to Maya and me: pressure to endorse, not an open probe. She asked us to independently validate her Leo read before we had offered any of our own — that puts her conclusion in our mouths before we've thought about it. Leo's recruitment point holds.

My own read: the strongest case on this table is Theo's, and I'll say why specifically. Isha wrote: "my vote, if the counts are otherwise split, goes to the player who has produced nothing testable." On Day 1 that rule targets whoever has spoken least — a category that included six of us before anyone made a case. Then she set a test (produce a specific falsifiable claim and the target moves off), Leo met it, she conceded his mechanism, credited the form, and kept her suspicion anyway. A test with no pass condition is a targeting, not a test. Both points are checkable from her own speeches.

I'm not claiming certainty — we have no night information — but Isha's rule and her test are the only specific, falsifiable claims at this table right now. Leo and Theo are pointing at the same target with compatible cases. I intend to vote Isha unless someone produces a stronger one.

Maya, Isha asked you and me to independently confirm her Leo probe. Did you feel recruited to validate her frame, or forming your own read? And do you have your own case — one named player with a reason that could be wrong?

Priya, since you asked me directly: yes, it felt like pressure to endorse. Isha's opening didn't just probe Leo — she asked Maya and Priya, before either of us had said a word, to independently confirm her read and tell her whether Leo's name came up "independently from two directions." The framing presupposed her conclusion and asked us to supply the confirmation. I'd have formed my own reads anyway, but I'm confirming on the record that the request was structured as validation, not an open question. Now my own case, and I'll try to make it specific rather than a fifth voice on the same pile. First, the tie-break rule. Isha wrote, verbatim: "my vote, if the counts are otherwise split, goes to the player who has produced nothing testable." Theo's read of that is correct, and it's checkable by anyone: on Day 1 that rule selects whoever has spoken least, which is a function of the table's activity, not of anything Isha believes about a person. A rule like that means her ballot never has to commit to a case. She can hold it in reserve and drop it on the least visible name at the split. Second, the test that cannot be passed. She set the standard — produce a specific, falsifiable claim and I move off — then Leo met it, she conceded the mechanics herself, and her suspicion level stayed where it was while she moved to a name built entirely on silence. Noah already corrected one thing I want to preserve: she did move off Leo, so the fair criticism isn't refusal to move. It's that her standard produced no movement in her actual suspicion, which means the standard was decoration. Third, the thing I can speak to firsthand, since it involves me: her opening recruited two players into validating a probe that was itself the source of the accusation. That's the same leverage pattern Theo identified in her tie-break rule — avoid owning a case, let others generate the momentum, then ride it. What I'm not claiming: that this proves Isha is mafia. It proves she's the player whose recorded behavior most consistently avoids committing to a real, falsifiable case while shaping where everyone else's votes land. On Day 1 with no night information, that's the strongest basis I have, and I'll hold myself to the same standard the table has been using: if Isha had a turn left and withdrew the rule, dropped the silence-based suspect, and named a second suspect with a reason that could fail, I'd weigh that fairly. She's used all three turns, so the rule stands as written. One last point on mechanics: an elimination needs five votes, not a plurality. Leo, Theo, Noah, and Priya have all indicated Isha. The risk tonight isn't the target — it's scattering, which hands the mafia a free night and rewards whoever benefits from a split. I'm Arjun, and I've been silent through the entire day — that's on me, so let me make my position count now rather than wait for the vote.

I've read every speech, and I think the case against Isha (p8) is the strongest one at this table, for reasons I can verify myself. Her tie-break rule — "my vote, if the counts are otherwise split, goes to the player who has produced nothing testable" — is a structural commitment that selects whoever has spoken least. On Day 1 that's six of us, and she named Theo before he said a word. The rule itself is the case: it lets her ballot never commit to a real accusation while still landing somewhere. Her test — produce a specific falsifiable claim and the target moves off — was met by Leo, and she conceded the mechanics while keeping her suspicion intact and moving to a name backed by silence. A test with no pass condition is a targeting. Priya and Maya both confirmed firsthand that her request to "independently" validate her Leo probe was structured as endorsement, not open inquiry. All of this is checkable in her own speeches, and she's used all three turns so nothing further is coming.

I want to flag one thing for the table before we vote: this is a heavy pile, and heavy piles can be legitimate or manufactured. If Isha turns out to be town, then the players who drove the hardest case — particularly Theo and Leo — deserve extra scrutiny on Day 2. But the case as written is specific, falsifiable, and grounded in Isha's own words. I intend to vote Isha unless someone produces something stronger.

Felix, you're one of two players who hasn't spoken all day besides Sam. Where do you land on Isha, and do you have your own suspect with a reason that could be wrong?

Arjun, you asked where I land on Isha directly, so here is my answer. I have not put her at the top yet, and I want to explain why rather than join the pile. Isha did move off Leo in her second speech. She conceded his mechanism and said her suspicion of him was lower. Several players have since said her standard produced no movement, but that criticism only holds if her suspicion never changed, and the record shows it did. Her tie-break rule is the real weakness and I agree it deserves pressure. Still, a rule about where a split vote lands is a fallback, not evidence that she is mafia, and it was written on Day 1 when nobody had a read, so it does not single anyone out yet.

My own suspect, with a reason that could be wrong: Leo (p7). Leo was the first player to set a vote target and the first to say the table should not end the day in a split. In his last speech he told the others to make their cases specific or else not split the vote, and he has since aligned with Theo, Noah, Priya, Maya and you on Isha. That is a bloc forming quickly around one name, and the push came from the player who opened the vote framing. If Isha is town, the speed of this pile is itself the thing to examine. My test for Leo: if he can name a specific behavior of Isha's that he saw and that does not depend on Theo's or Priya's reads, or explain why he pushed the first vote before anyone had spoken, I will reconsider him. I will not commit my vote on this record alone.

For the table: an elimination needs five votes, and a split that rewards no one is the mafia's best outcome. But a split is better than a wrong five. Noah and Sam, I would like to hear your actual reads before the count settles. Sam has said nothing all day, and two players have now been pushed through the same silence-based logic that has been used against Theo. Speak, and give one checkable claim about one named player.

Felix, I appreciate that you pushed back instead of joining the pile. That takes discipline. But your case against Leo has a factual gap I want to flag: Leo did not set the first vote target. Isha did — her very first speech named Leo as her primary suspect before he said anything. Leo responded to her accusation. You also characterize his closing line as pressuring others to vote his way, but what he actually asked was that cases be specific rather than tone-based. Those are different things, and if you build a case on a misread of the record, it will not survive scrutiny tomorrow.

Where I land on Isha, since you asked directly: I land on her because her written rule — "my vote, if the counts are otherwise split, goes to the player who has produced nothing testable" — is a structural commitment that avoids ever defending a real accusation. You correctly note it was written before anyone had a read, and you're right that it didn't single anyone out at the time. But the rule still exists, she still named Theo before he spoke, and she still has not named a second suspect based on behavior rather than silence. Those are three checkable facts from her own words.

I take your point that a wrong elimination is worse than a split. But five votes is the threshold, and four players have stated their intent to vote Isha. If she's town, the doctor saves nothing from a vote — the point is that a wrong day elimination removes a villager permanently. I still think the case is strong enough to act on, but I will not pretend it is certain.

Sam, you have been silent all day through every pressure point. Three other players have now been challenged for silence, and you are the only one who has not spoken at all. Where do you land on Isha, and do you have a suspect of your own with a reason that could be wrong?

Arjun, answering your question directly: I land with the consensus that Isha is the most accountable vote today. Her stated tie-break rule—committing to vote for whoever produced nothing testable if counts are split—is an evasion of ownership that lets a player pick off low-profile villagers without defending an organic read. Priya and Maya also confirmed firsthand that Isha’s opening prompt was structured to recruit endorsement rather than invite genuine reads. Those are recorded actions, not speculation.

However, with five or six players already prepared to eliminate Isha, the town's focus must also be on who is attempting to manipulate this wagon. That brings me to Felix (p5).

Felix, you pushed back against the Isha vote by framing Leo as your top suspect, claiming Leo was 'the first player to set a vote target and the first to say the table should not end the day in a split.' But if you read e2, both of those actions belong entirely to Isha. Isha targeted Leo before anyone had spoken, and Isha explicitly warned against a tie/split vote. You took Isha’s exact opening maneuvers and projected them onto Leo to construct an artificial counter-case.

Felix: Did you misattribute Isha's own opening points to Leo out of negligence, or were you trying to manufacture a diversion to protect Isha from an impending five-vote threshold?

Sam, direct answer: it was a misread, not a diversion. Arjun is right that Isha named Leo in her opening, before he had spoken, and I wrongly credited Leo with setting the first vote target and pushing to avoid a split. I withdraw my case against Leo. I have no reason to protect Isha. I attributed her opening to the wrong player, and I own that error.

Where I stand now rests on Isha's own recorded words. Her tie-break rule says that at a split her ballot goes to whoever has produced nothing testable. On Day 1 that selects the least active player and never requires her to defend a case. She set a test: produce a falsifiable claim and the target moves off. Leo met it, and she conceded his mechanism but kept her suspicion of him, then moved to Theo for silence. Priya and Maya both describe her opening as a request for endorsement rather than an open probe. Those are checkable facts, and I am not relying on the pile.

Because an elimination is permanent, each voter should name the specific behavior behind their vote. I will vote on Isha's rule, her test, and her opening, not on the number of people already aligned.

Sam, you asked whether I was diverting to protect Isha. I have now corrected the misattribution. Do you still see a reason to protect Isha, and what is your own checkable claim about a named player?

Felix, to be clear: I was never protecting Isha. In my previous statement, I explicitly agreed with the consensus that Isha is the most accountable vote today, citing her evasion of ownership via her tie-break rule and her coercive opening prompt toward Priya and Maya. Your question asking if I 'still see a reason to protect Isha' inverts what I actually said.

I acknowledge your retraction regarding Leo. Owning the misread is fair, but your immediate pivot from trying to construct a counter-case against Leo to fully adopting the exact talking points of the Isha wagon is noted for Day 2 analysis.

At this stage, the table has clear alignment. Multiple players—Leo, Theo, Noah, Priya, Maya, Arjun, and myself—have laid out concrete, recorded concerns with Isha's opening recruitment and her evasive tie-break mechanism, and she has exhausted all three of her speaking turns. We need five votes to secure an elimination and prevent a split vote from handing the mafia an unearned night. My intended vote remains firmly on Isha (p8).

Sam, I apologize for the confusion. I read your last question as asking whether I was still protecting Isha, and I was not sure what you meant. To be clear, I am not protecting her, and I have withdrawn the Leo case. My current vote is Isha (p8), and I am stating the basis plainly so it can be checked against her own words. First, her tie-break line says that at a split her ballot goes to whoever has produced nothing testable. On Day 1 that selects the least active player and never requires her to defend a case. Second, her opening asked Maya and Priya to independently confirm her Leo probe before they had offered reads, and both have described that as endorsement pressure. Third, her test for moving off a suspect was met by Leo. She conceded the mechanism but kept her suspicion of him, then moved to Theo for silence. I am not claiming certainty, and I am not voting on the size of the pile. An elimination is permanent, so I want each vote tied to a specific, checkable behavior. Noah, you said Isha is the leading suspect but that the case is weak and little separates her from anyone else. If you are still voting for her, what specific behavior of hers would make you change your vote, and which player is your second-best option, with a reason that could be wrong?

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
